newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's 1998 budget plans start to take shape.
newsitem.headline: Italy's 1998 budget plans start to take shape.

text.p: Italy looks set to unveil the bare bones of a 1998 budget this week seeking 25 trillion lire ($14 billion) of deficit-cutting measures -- enough on paper to meet a key European monetary union criterion, analysts say.
Treasury undersecretary Giorgio Macciotta said last week Italy needs a deficit-cutting budget of around 25 trillion lire for 1998 to meet conditions for EMU membership.

Analysts expect budget targets to be contained in the government's annual document of three-year rolling economic targets known as the Dpef which the cabinet of Prime Minister Romano Prodi is likely to examine by the end of the week.

Italian newspapers, which analysts say often have accurate economic data before official figures are released, gave a more detailed breakdown at the weekend, predicting 17 trillion lire of spending cuts and eight trillion of higher revenues to pare the budget deficit in 1998.

"From what we learned from the press close to half the 1998 package should be accounted for by spending cuts on pensions, health care and by a hike in VAT (value added tax) rates," said Riccardo Barbieri, senior economist at Morgan Stanley in London.
Andrea Cecchini, economist at Banque Indosuez in Milan said the figures quoted in newspapers were sufficient to meet a key Maastricht criterion for taking part in a single currency."
"But we still need to know if the majority (supporting the government in parliament) is willing to vote for this financial document," he said.

The ruling centre-left coalition has a majority in the upper house or Senate. But in the lower house it relies on the support of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, which is adamantly opposed to cuts in welfare spending.

Barbieri said the presentation of some components of the 1998 budget in the Dpef could provoke objections from some members of the coalition. "The document will provide a first test of how the debate will shape up as the budget session approaches (later this year)."

He said the government had tried before to surprise markets with bigger measures than suggested by press reports. "But in this case presenting a high figure would be counterproductive. The government must go for something that's feasible politically but which makes sense as a projection," he said.
Weekend reports forecast eight trillion lire of spending cuts through welfare reforms, with five to six trillion of that coming from savings in the pensions system.
A further 3.7 trillion was expected from reforms to public administration and the rest from other reductions in spending.

Bringing VAT tax rates into line with other European countries would cut the budget deficit by a further four to five trillion lire. The overall revenue-raising measures were broadly seen bringing in a total of eight trillion lire.

Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas in London called the 25 trillion lire "sizeable but towards the bottom end of expectations" but added that Italy's political problems tended to start when the budget process got down to details.
The Dpef usually gives a broad outline of targets for the next three years, leaving the details to the actual budget law, which has to be presented to parliament by the end of September.

But Prodi is under pressure to show quickly that he can take tough and credible measures in order to silence EU partners who doubt Italy's credentials for joining Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) at its January 1999 start.

Italy has already been criticised for resorting to one-off measures to force this year's deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio down to the three percent required to join EMU. That ratio was 6.7 percent in 1996 and EU partners want Italy to take steps to reduce structural spending on pensions and welfare.
